prompt: The complexity classes P and NP — which two statements are correct?
options: A problem is in P if a deterministic algorithm solves it in polynomial worst-case time.
P ⊆ NP always holds, since a poly-time solver also serves as a poly-time verifier.
NP is defined as the class of problems that provably cannot be solved in polynomial time.
P = NP has been proven, which is why NP-complete problems are considered hard.
explanation: The definition of P ✓ and the trivial inclusion P ⊆ NP ✓ (just ignore the certificate and solve it yourself) are standard. NP is about *verifiability*, not about proven hardness ✗, and P vs. NP is famously still open — a Millennium Problem ✗.

prompt: What does it mean for a problem to be NP-hard without necessarily being in NP?
options: It is easier than the NP-complete problems.
Every problem in NP reduces to it in polynomial time, but its own solutions need not be verifiable in polynomial time.
It has already been proven unsolvable.
It is automatically also in P.
explanation: NP-hard means only "at least as hard as everything in NP" via polynomial reduction — membership in NP is a separate requirement. NP-complete = NP-hard *and* in NP, so an NP-hard problem outside NP is at least as hard as, never easier than, the NP-complete ones.

prompt: Polynomial-time reduction L₁ ≤_P L₂ — which two statements are correct?
options: There is a poly-time computable f with x ∈ L₁ ⟺ f(x) ∈ L₂.
≤_P is transitive: L₁ ≤_P L₂ and L₂ ≤_P L₃ imply L₁ ≤_P L₃ via the composition f₂ ∘ f₁.
L₁ ≤_P L₂ means L₁ is at least as hard as L₂.
A reduction does not carry over to the complements: L₁ ≤_P L₂ says nothing about L̄₁ and L̄₂.
explanation: The definition ✓ and transitivity via composition ✓ are what make "one for all, all for one" work. The direction in option 3 is inverted — L₂ is at least as hard as L₁ ✗ — and negating both sides of the equivalence gives L̄₁ ≤_P L̄₂ with the *same* f ✗.

prompt: Consequences of NP-completeness — which two statements are correct?
options: If a single NP-complete problem lies in P, then P = NP.
If some problem in NP is not solvable in polynomial time, then no NP-complete problem is.
If a single NP-complete problem lies in P, only the problems reducible to it become efficient.
SAT is NP-complete, but every other NP-completeness proof must likewise be carried out directly via Cook-Levin.
explanation: Chaining a poly-time reduction with a poly-time solver makes every NP problem poly-time ✓, and option 2 is exactly its contrapositive ✓. Option 3 misses that *every* NP problem reduces to an NP-complete one ✗, and after Cook-Levin, new proofs chain off an already-known NP-complete problem ✗.

options: 2-SAT is in P (via implication graphs and SCCs); 3-SAT is NP-complete.
Both are NP-complete.
Both are in P.
3-SAT is in P; 2-SAT is NP-complete.
explanation: A 2-literal clause (a ∨ b) is equivalent to the implications ¬a → b and ¬b → a, so satisfiability reduces to a strongly-connected-components check on the implication graph — polynomial. Three literals per clause interlink variables in a way that resists this local shortcut; 3-SAT is the canonical NP-complete problem.

prompt: Which pair correctly matches (polynomial problem, NP-complete problem)?
options: 2-colourability (bipartiteness) is in P; 3-colourability is NP-complete.
3-colourability is in P; 2-colourability is NP-complete.
Both are in P.
Both are NP-complete.
explanation: With two colours, colouring one vertex deterministically forces all its neighbours, so a single BFS/DFS decides it in O(V+E). With three colours each neighbour retains two open options, producing a genuinely exponential branching search. 3-colourability is one of Karp's original 21 NP-complete problems.

prompt: Shortest versus longest simple path — which two statements are correct?
options: The shortest simple path is in P, e.g. via Dijkstra or Bellman-Ford.
The longest simple path is NP-complete, because avoiding revisits destroys the optimal substructure.
Both problems are in P, since both can be solved with the same relaxation technique.
The longest simple path is in P, because one can simply negate all edge weights and run Dijkstra.
explanation: Shortest paths have optimal substructure that DP and greedy exploit ✓; the longest *simple* path must reason about exponentially many vertex subsets to avoid revisits, which breaks that substructure ✓. Negating weights produces negative edges Dijkstra cannot handle, and negative cycles for Bellman-Ford ✗✗.

prompt: Proving HAM-PATH ∈ NP with the certificate p = (v₁, …, vₙ): which of the four verifier conditions dominates the O(V²) total verification time?
options: Checking that all vertices in p are pairwise distinct
Checking that p contains the right number of vertices
Checking that every vᵢ is a vertex of G
Checking that every consecutive pair (vᵢ, vᵢ₊₁) is an edge of G
explanation: Pairwise distinctness compares up to O(V²) pairs in the worst case. The other three are each a single O(V) pass over the certificate. Since all four together are exactly the definition of a Hamiltonian path, the verifier is correct — and polynomial, which is what membership in NP requires.

prompt: Hamiltonian Path restricted to directed acyclic graphs — which two statements are correct?
options: In a DAG a Hamiltonian path must follow the topological order, so there is exactly one candidate to check.
The decision therefore costs O(V+E): topologically sort, then test whether every consecutive pair is an edge.
DAGs never have a Hamiltonian path, so the answer is trivially always "no".
This contradicts the NP-completeness of the general problem.
explanation: A path cannot move against the edge directions without revisiting a vertex, so the topological order is the only possible candidate ✓, making the check O(V+E) ✓. DAGs certainly can have Hamiltonian paths ✗, and a restricted special case being easy never contradicts general-case hardness ✗.

prompt: How should one deal with a problem shown to be NP-complete? Which two statements are correct?
options: Use approximation algorithms — e.g. a random assignment satisfies an expected ≥ ½ of all 3SAT clauses.
Check whether the concrete instance falls into a polynomial special case, such as Hamiltonian Path on a DAG.
Keep searching for an exact polynomial algorithm — one is simply not known yet for the specific instance.
Since no algorithm exists at all, the problem is undecidable.
explanation: Approximation ✓ and exploiting structural special cases ✓ are two of the four standard escapes (heuristics and pruned exponential search are the others). Finding an exact poly-time algorithm would prove P = NP ✗, and NP-complete problems are perfectly decidable — just not known to be efficiently so ✗.
